transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Soto (CTO, Verdant), Marcus Lin (Head of IT), Priya Raman (Security Lead), Jordan Brooks (Bioinformatics)

Summary:
Quick discovery for Verdant Diagnostics' interest in an on‑prem, air‑gapped deployment of Redwood Private. Main concerns: offline updates, hardware profile (NVIDIA A100 vs H100 vs CPU fallback), KMS/HSM integration, SOC2/ISO evidence, and pilot benchmarks for latency and throughput on a constrained rack environment. Customer also asked about model packaging, quantization options, and support SLAs.

Topics:
- On‑prem air‑gapped deployment model and expected operational processes
- Offline update mechanics and secure transfer protocols
- Hardware constraints and recommended GPU profiles/quantization strategy
- Security/compliance: KMS, HSM, RBAC, audit logs, SSO
- Pilot scope, success criteria, timeline, and pricing

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Maya, AE on the account, and Ravi my colleague from SE will run through the technical stuff. Elena, Marcus, Priya — nice to meet you. Could you do quick intros?
[00:23] Dr. Elena Soto: Yeah hi, Elena here. CTO at Verdant. We're moving a bunch of inference workloads in‑house because of regulatory privacy concerns for patient genomic data.
[00:37] Marcus Lin: Marcus, head of IT. I'll be responsible for the infra and the ops side of any on‑prem deployment.
[00:44] Priya Raman: Priya, security. Looking closely at encryption, airgap processes, and auditability.
[00:50] Jordan Brooks: Jordan, bioinformatics. I'll be managing test datasets for the pilot.
[00:55] Ravi Patel: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: we'll cover our Private on‑prem offering, how we handle air‑gapped updates, hardware guidance, and then dig into pilot scope and next steps.

[02:10] Marcus Lin: Quick question up front — what's the minimum hardware you recommend? We're limited to two racks right now, power and cooling are tight.
[02:25] Ravi Patel: Totally. For production across high‑throughput batch inference we recommend at least NVIDIA A100‑40GB or equivalent. H100s are preferred if you want best fp16/quant performance, but for constrained racks we support quantized models that run on A100 or even T4s for lower throughput. There is also a CPU fallback but expect significant latency.
[03:05] Marcus Lin: You mentioned quantization — do you ship the quantized artifacts or do we run the quantization on‑prem?
[03:18] Ravi Patel: Good question. We have two modes: Redwood can deliver a pre‑compiled quantized bundle that you import into the private runtime (helps for air‑gapped installs), or we can provide the quant toolchain and scripts to run internally. For air‑gapped customers, most prefer pre‑signed bundles and a verification hash mechanism.
[04:00] Priya Raman: How do you handle updates? We cannot have outbound network access.
[04:12] Maya Chen: Right — for air‑gapped sites our process is an offline update bundle. We sign bundles with Redwood's private key, you verify signatures with your copy of our public key, and then you load via a secure USB or internal transfer. We also support a pull model via an approved jump server for customers who have an approved egress path.
[04:45] Priya Raman: What about KMS and HSM? We use an enterprise HSM and strict key custody.
[04:53] Ravi Patel: We integrate with customer HSMs via PKCS#11. For air‑gapped setups we provide an HSM connector that runs in the private control plane and only communicates locally. Keys never leave your HSM; Redwood's runtime can call the PKCS#11 interface for signing and decryption. We also support bringing your own key pairs for bundle verification.
[05:30] Dr. Elena Soto: Can you talk about onboarding — how long to get a pilot running?
[05:40] Maya Chen: Typical pilot is 4–6 weeks: week 1 — environment review and hardware validation; week 2 — install and smoke tests; week 3 — benchmark runs and tuning; week 4 — iterate on quality/latency and handover. Given air‑gap and change control, plan for a couple extra weeks for security approvals.
[06:10] Marcus Lin: About the install — what's required on the host side? Do we need an orchestrator like k8s?
[06:20] Ravi Patel: Our Private package can run standalone on a host OS with systemd units for the runtime, or you can deploy inside k8s. For smaller footprints we recommend the standalone runtime with a lightweight process supervisor to keep the stack simple inside air‑gapped networks.
[06:50] Jordan Brooks: From a data perspective, we need to run our variant calling prompts and some long‑context models. Any sequence length limits we should be aware of?
[07:05] Ravi Patel: Our runtime supports long context models with optimized KV cache handling. There are practical memory limits depending on model and batch sizes — we'll size the GPU memory accordingly. For long prompts we may recommend model variants with attention optimizations or offload to larger GPUs. We'll include a sizing worksheet in the security pack.
[07:45] Priya Raman: SOC2 and ISO evidence — do you have artifacts we can share with our auditors?
[07:55] Maya Chen: Yes, we have SOC2 Type II report, ISO27001 cert summary, and an on‑prem security checklist. We'll attach non‑disclosure redacted reports in the package. For Private, the control plane for air‑gapped installs is customer‑managed so audit scope is focused on our delivered software and the deployment process.
[08:30] Marcus Lin: License model — is it subscription, perpetual, or a mix?
[08:40] Maya Chen: Typically Private is a subscription per cluster or per reserved capacity, plus an initial install and support fee. We can discuss enterprise licensing if you need perpetual options; I'll include pricing bands in the follow up.

[10:00] Elena Soto: Our main success criteria for pilot: 1) latency under 120ms p50 for our typical prompts, 2) throughput of at least 10 qps for batch pipelines, and 3) no data exfiltration — strict audit logs. Are those doable?
[10:20] Ravi Patel: They are realistic. We'll propose a pilot that measures p50/p95 latency across representative prompts, throughput with configured batching, and run a security verification checklist to validate no egress and correct audit logging.

[12:00] Marcus Lin: On the airgap verification — can we run hash verification and deterministic builds? We need to check binary integrity before install.
[12:12] Ravi Patel: Absolutely. All bundles are signed and we publish SHA‑256 hashes. For greater assurance we can provide reproducible build artifacts and build logs under NDA.

[13:05] Priya Raman: Who from Redwood will be on call for incident support during pilot? We need escalation paths and SLA details.
[13:15] Maya Chen: For pilots we provide a dedicated SE (Ravi) for technical, and AE (me) for commercial/coordination. For production customers we offer 24/7 support add‑ons with defined response times and an enterprise escalation ladder. I'll include the support SLO doc.

[15:20] Jordan Brooks: For the models — do you support Open models only, or can we bring custom models? We have internally trained models for variant annotation.
[15:34] Ravi Patel: You can bring your own models. We support a model packaging format for customer models and will help with quantization and kernel selection. For proprietary models we recommend keeping model files within your enclave and using our private runtime to serve them; we never copy models out of your cluster.

[17:00] Marcus Lin: What's the typical disk footprint for an H100 quantized model and the runtime? We have limited storage on some nodes.
[17:10] Ravi Patel: Quantized models can be significantly smaller (2–4x) depending on your quant setting; an Llama‑class 30B quant model can be under 40–60GB in certain 4‑bit formats. The runtime itself is small — a few hundred MB — but you'll want local NVMe scratch for caching and logs. We'll provide detailed sizing per model.

[19:00] Elena Soto: Any concerns around IP and model provenance? Our legal team wants guarantees that deployed models are not exfiltrated.
[19:12] Maya Chen: We provide contractual protections and technical controls: no outbound telemetry by default, signed bundles, and you can run in a fully air‑gapped mode. We can instrument audit logs and provide redactions for telemetry; telemetry is opt‑in for Private installs.

[21:30] Priya Raman: For KMS, do you support rotated keys and offline rotation procedures?
[21:40] Ravi Patel: Yes. Keys can be rotated locally; our tooling supports offline rotation with signed rotation manifests. We'll document the recommended rotation cadence and procedures in the security pack.

[24:00] Marcus Lin: Let's talk about benchmarks — do you have a template for the test harness?
[24:12] Ravi Patel: Yes, we have a benchmark harness that runs throughput and latency tests with configurable prompt sets and batch sizes. For the pilot we'll tailor it to Jordan's prompts and include scripts you can run offline. We'll also collect per‑token latency breakdowns and GPU utilization.

[26:00] Jordan Brooks: We sometimes need streaming responses and tool‑calling — is that supported in air‑gapped Private?
[26:12] Ravi Patel: Streaming is supported; function/tool calling depends on whether the tool endpoints are reachable. In an air‑gapped setup you can host tool endpoints inside your network; Redwood supports internal routing to local tool endpoints.

[28:30] Elena Soto: Are there any known limitations running in strict air‑gapped mode vs Hosted?
[28:40] Ravi Patel: Main limitations are around convenience for updates and external telemetry/analytics. Features that require cloud connectivity — e.g., hosted model catalog live updates — will be replaced by offline bundles. Also, some advanced autoscaling features are different because they rely on control‑plane coordination. But core inference, batching, caching, and fallbacks all run offline.

[31:00] Priya Raman: Do you support RBAC and SSO integrations for our internal users?
[31:10] Maya Chen: Yes, SSO via SAML/OIDC is supported and maps to RBAC roles in the private control plane. We'll give examples of role bindings in the install guide.

[33:00] Marcus Lin: If we need to do firmware upgrades or kernel patches, do you recommend downtime windows?
[33:12] Ravi Patel: Yes, we recommend maintenance windows for kernel or driver upgrades. For live production you can run a canary host and drain traffic, but in a tight rack we may need scheduled downtime. We'll help design a rollout plan with canaries if you want zero‑downtime goals.

[35:20] Elena Soto: Cost perspective — balancing H100 vs A100 and quantization. We need a TCO estimate for 12 months.
[35:34] Maya Chen: We'll include a TCO workbook that compares raw hardware spend, licensing, and expected token compute cost using Redwood Optimize recommendations. Quantization and batching knobs can reduce cost significantly; we'll show a few scenarios.

[38:00] Jordan Brooks: For data access controls — can the runtime enforce field‑level masking before logs are written?
[38:12] Ravi Patel: Yes, we can plug in transformation hooks to sanitize or redact sensitive fields pre‑log. That runs in the runtime and is configurable.

[40:00] Priya Raman: Any reference customers for on‑prem air‑gapped deployments in healthcare?
[40:10] Maya Chen: We can provide references under NDA — we've done similar engagements for two mid‑sized diagnostic labs and a hospital research group. I'll request permission to share contact info; otherwise we'll share anonymized case studies.

[42:30] Marcus Lin: One more practical — what's the upgrade cadence for the runtime?
[42:40] Ravi Patel: We release quarterly updates; air‑gapped customers get signed offline bundles aligned to that cadence, but you choose when to install. Security patches can be issued as hotfix bundles when needed.

[45:00] Elena Soto: Let's talk pilot success criteria again — we want clear go/no‑go gates.
[45:12] Maya Chen: Agreed. Proposed gates: 1) Benchmarks meet p50/p95 targets, 2) Security checklist items validated (KMS, audit logs, bundle verification), 3) Ops runbook and rollback validated, 4) Stakeholder signoff on cost and SLA. We'll draft a short pilot acceptance doc.

[47:20] Marcus Lin: Timing — we need to line up procurement approvals. If we start approvals this week, when could pilot start?
[47:30] Maya Chen: If approvals clear in two weeks, we can start a pilot kickoff the week of 2026‑10‑19. That fits into the 4–6 week pilot window and a production decision before year end if all goes well.

[50:00] Priya Raman: A few technical clarifications for the security pack: we need network diagrams, expected firewall rules, and the offline bundle verification steps spelled out.
[50:12] Maya Chen: We'll include a network diagram template, recommended firewall/IP ranges, default ports for internal components, and a step‑by‑step offline bundle verification guide.

[52:20] Jordan Brooks: For model performance regressions — do you provide quality monitoring or eval tooling?
[52:32] Ravi Patel: Yes. Redwood Optimize includes evaluation harnesses and quality monitors tied to prompt sets; for Private we'll ship a local eval runner and threshold alerts that integrate with your on‑prem monitoring.

[54:00] Elena Soto: Great. Any final questions?
[54:10] Priya Raman: One last: can we run a compliance dry‑run where your team simulates an audit to make sure we have the evidence?
[54:22] Maya Chen: We can – our professional services group will run a compliance runbook dry‑run for an add‑on fee. I'll include options in the follow up.

[55:00] Maya Chen: Ok recap — I'll send SOC2 + security pack, pricing bands, and an install checklist by Monday (2026‑10‑04). Ravi will draft the benchmark/pilot plan and share scripts. Marcus will send hardware inventory and constraints. Priya to confirm compliance gatekeepers. We'll aim to kick off the pilot mid‑October assuming approvals.
[55:45] Dr. Elena Soto: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[55:50] Marcus Lin: Thanks, talk soon.
[55:53] Ravi Patel: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the docs and next steps.

End of transcript.
